extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory; readers of Montesquieu and classical political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated commentary on Montesquieu's classification and principles of government, extracting the normative criteria he and his commentators use to evaluate laws, regimes, and political institutions. Focuses on nature/principle distinctions, requirements for different regimes, and civic virtues and institutions that sustain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternal justice vs circumstantial justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether there is an eternal and absolute justice, or whether justice is only the result of circumstances (Note C10: 'Il s'agit de savoir s'il y a une justice éternelle et absolue, ou si elle n'est que le résultat des circonstances.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a central philosophical criterion: one must decide whether normative claims (justice) are universal or contingent on historical/social conditions. The commentary notes the importance of the dispute (réaux vs nominaux) and treats it as substantive rather than frivolous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of human deviation from laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's explanation: intelligent beings do not always follow laws not only because of their limited nature, but because they possess freedom ('ce n'est pas seulement parce que les êtres intelligents sont bornés... c'est encore parce qu'ils ont la liberté') (Note C11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both boundedness (limitations of nature) and freedom are necessary to explain human errors; neither alone suffices. This is an explanatory criterion for assessing human compliance with law and the role of liberty in political behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals: automata vs spontaneous movers
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether animals are governed by general mechanical laws (automata, à la Descartes) or by particular, spontaneous motion (Note C12: 'On ne sait si les bêtes sont gouvernées par les lois générales du mouvement ou par une motion particulière.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish kinds of natural law and to show the contrast between mechanistic determinism and internal principles; illustrative of whether a domain is governed by impersonal laws or by internal agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural laws of animals vs positive laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals possess 'lois naturelles' (laws of organization and instinct) which are physical, but do not possess 'lois positives' (written laws born of human will and convention) because they lack freedom and speech (Note C13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for distinguishing types of law: positive laws presuppose capacity for agreement and language. Example/anti-pattern: animals cannot have conventions because they lack signs/speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: 'lois de la nature' vs 'loi naturelle'
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu distinguishes 'lois de la nature' (instinctive, physical laws) from the 'loi naturelle' of moral philosophy (innate law of justice), and enumerates four natural laws: inclination toward the Creator, toward sex, need of nourishment, and need of society (Note C14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides evaluation of claims about 'natural law' by requiring clarity about whether one means biological instincts or moral reason; provides Montesquieu's list of what counts as natural instincts to be considered when reconstructing a hypothetical state of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of nature: war vs pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes' claim that the natural state is 'war of all against all' is contrasted with Montesquieu (and Rousseau) who argue that primitive human sentiment was not war but pity (Note C16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for assessing theories of political origins: examine empirical signs (e.g., whether animals living in groups show intra-group war) and alternative philosophical reconstructions; use historical and biological analogies cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of political power (paternal vs contractual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filmer's doctrine: political power originates in paternal power (from Adam), transmitted by lineage; critics (Sidney, Locke, Rousseau) refute this in favor of contractual or other origins (Note C18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about legitimacy, test whether they rest on hereditary/patriarchal metaphors or on consent and contract; consider historical refutations and counter-arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of government to people's disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental axiom: 'Le gouvernement le plus conforme à la nature est celui qui se rapporte le mieux à la disposition du peuple pour lequel il est établi.' (Note C19). There is no single best government; forms must suit social conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a design principle: choose or evaluate institutions by their fit to population's social state, climate, customs, and dispositions rather than seeking a universal form. Applies equally to monarchy and republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as human reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's claim: 'La loi en général est la raison humaine...' — laws substitute the reign of reason for brute force, anticipate conflicts and regulate them according to justice and common interest (Note C20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for legislation: does a law express reason, foresee conflicts, and pursue justice and the common interest? Laws should be judged by their rational grounding and purpose (to promote peace over war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit of laws: relation to circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'esprit des lois' is the study of laws in relation to all circumstances that modify them (government, climate, mode of life, political freedom, religion, commerce, manners) (Note C21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic approach: when analyzing a law or institution, consider the full range of modifying circumstances; anti-pattern: treating laws as isolated from their environmental and social causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by number and purpose of governors
rubrics_metrics.description: Three species of government: by one, by several, by the multitude; each can be good (aim at public good) or corrupt (serve rulers' interest), yielding royauté/monarchy, aristocratie, république or their corrupt forms tyranny/oligarchy/démagogue (Note C22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this two-axis classification (who rules × whose interest) to evaluate constitutions; check both structure (number) and governance purpose (public vs private interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature vs principle of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: nature of government = what makes it exist (its structure); principle = what makes it act (the passions or motivating forces) — 'sa nature est ce qui le fait être et son principe ce qui le fait agir' (Note C23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing a regime, separate its formal institutions (nature) from the social/political motives that animate behavior (principle); many laws follow from this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy and sovereignty (Rousseau's influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rousseau's formulations: definitions of democracy where the people as sovereign can be both magistrates and subjects; sovereignty lies in the 'volonté générale' — 'La volonté du souverain est le souverain lui-même.' (Notes C24-C26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for democratic legitimacy: existence of collective will expressed as general will; in evaluating democratic designs, consider how sovereignty is constituted and whether representation preserves or dilutes the general will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative competence of people vs prince
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument (Machiavel cited): the people generally err less in choosing magistrates than a small elite or a single prince — 'Vous verrez toujours moins d'erreurs dans le peuple que dans le prince' (Note C27).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify wider participation in selection of officials; when assessing selection mechanisms, weigh aggregate judgment vs concentrated selection for error frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sortition is not intrinsic to democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Montesquieu: 'Le suffrage par le sort est de la nature de la démocratie' is false; democracy should be enlightened, not blind — sortition was criticized by Socrates/Plato (Note C29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate electoral methods: random selection may conflict with the aim of choosing talent; prefer deliberative or competence-based selection mechanisms unless sortition is specifically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs secret voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's claim that suffrages must be public is disputed: modern democracies favor secret ballots to protect freedom; representatives' votes should be known except in special cases (Note C30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing electoral rules, balance transparency (constitutive for representatives) and voter protection (secret ballot to avoid coercion); context-sensitive: elections vs parliamentary votes differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the people vs representative lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Contestable claim: 'C'est une loi fondamentale de la démocratie que le peuple seul fasse des lois.' The commentary argues this ignores representative government—modern democracies use representation and bicameralism (Note C31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for constitutional design: determine whether legislative authority is direct (popular lawmaking) or representative; assess legitimacy of delegated legislative mechanisms in light of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Including popular element under aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable in aristocracy to make indirect provision for the people's participation to avoid their annihilation — 'Ce sera une chose heureuse dans l'aristocratie si par quelque voie indirecte, on fait sortir le peuple de son anéantissement.' (Note C32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recommendation: aristocratic regimes should incorporate channels for popular influence (e.g., appointments, access to functions) to maintain stability and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary concentration of power in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges that a concentrated power (dictatorship) may be necessary in extreme cases but must be brief — 'compense la grandeur de la puissance par la brièveté de la durée' (Note C33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional principle: allow emergency powers only under strict temporal limits; modern constitutions avoid permanent dictatorships because they encourage abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy improved by popular openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: 'Plus une aristocratie approchera de la démocratie, plus elle sera parfaite.' Openness to popular elements strengthens aristocracy (Note C34).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design: broaden recruitment and access to aristocratic offices to secure public trust and longevity; anti-pattern: closed elites that isolate themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediary powers as essence of monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers intermédiaires (Parlements, Nobility, Clergy, city corporations) constitute the nature of a monarchy; their abolition leads to despotism (Note C35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for monarchy: presence of intermediate bodies that check royal will indicates a true monarchy; absence of such checks is a red flag for despotism or arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual dependence of monarch and nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxim: 'Point de monarque, point de noblesse; Point de noblesse, point de monarque.' The nobility is one of the channels through which monarchical power flows; removing their prerogatives produces despotism (Notes C36-C37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as historical-institutional criterion: assess whether weakening intermediary elites has pushed a polity toward despotism or popular upheaval; interpret changes in social channels as causal for regime transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament as 'dépôt des lois'
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's notion that there must be a 'dépôt de lois' — a body that announces and recalls laws (the Parliament) (Note C40).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional standard: law-preserving and law-interpreting bodies (parliaments/registrars) are necessary to maintain legal continuity and public memory; absence undermines legal stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism as abuse, not a form
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism is characterized as an abuse of government forms, not a distinct essence; differences between monarchy and despotism are often degrees rather than separate kinds (Notes C41, C54).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic caution: classify despotism by presence of arbitrary rule and lack of institutional constraint rather than by formal labels; recognize cross-form tyranny (democratic despotism, aristocratic tyranny, monarchical despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as principle of democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine: 'La vertu est le principe des démocraties'; civic/ political virtue (love of liberty, respect for laws and magistrates, sense of equality) is essential for republican success and more required than in other governments (Notes C43-C44, C57).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion for republican stability: measure the prevalence of civic virtue and education; recommend prioritizing education and civic inculcation as central ministries and policies. Anti-pattern: reliance solely on legal coercion where civic virtue is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of education in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: republics (U.S., Switzerland, modern France) place education at the forefront of public concerns; education should be aligned with social conditions and civic needs (Notes C58, C63).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: invest in public education and align curricula to prepare citizens for political life; use educational institutions to cultivate civic virtues necessary for republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation as the soul of aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle that moderation characterizes aristocratic government and is a virtue in all regimes — avoid excess of power or liberty (Note C47).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative test: assess whether institutions embody moderation (balance of powers, limits on extremes); anti-pattern: extremes in authority or license that destabilize the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and distinctions as principles of monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion: the principle of monarchy is 'l'honneur' — honor consists in preferences and distinctions and is more prevalent in monarchies than democracies (Notes C51, C52).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating monarchical systems, consider the role of honorific distinctions in motivating elites and structuring society; note that democratizing pressures reduce such distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate customs by circumstances and intended ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the Lacedaemonian permitted theft by youths is judged according to its context and aims (training, scarcity, legal constraints) rather than by universal condemnation (Note C65).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rule: judge institutions and customs with attention to their purposes, historical context, and consequences; avoid decontextualized moral condemnation. Use empirical/historical sources (Plutarch, Rollin) to inform assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions on analogical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against arbitrary or inapt analogies (e.g., comparing Penn's Quaker colony to Lycurgue's Sparta is 'tout à fait arbitraire') (Note C67).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic guideline: when drawing historical or cross-cultural analogies, verify core similarities (ends, constraints, social structure); avoid superficial parallels that mislead institutional interpretation.
